title: We Who Chase the Stars
subtitle: Those who departed from home are now wandering through tales.

trails.title: Cabinet of Wishes
trails.description: New Year's wishes made when the Kremlin's bells ring are kept here, ready to be laughed at next year.

content.text:
Become Director. Drink endless wine. Succeed in projects.

World peace. Conquer the galaxy. Go home for a visit.

Live to see next year. Touch Mars with your own hands. Establish relations with alien life.

Grow flowers in Siberia. Free yourself from material needs. Become a true engineer.

Defeat death. Marry Anastasia. Witness history.

items.text: The hardest person to convince is often yourself.
Sensing Kiperina's disappointment, Name Day finally speaks up.

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: About that ...

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: I don't know.
The blunt reply causes him to bite his tongue and listen.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: When I heard about my parents' deaths, I was just stepping onto the bus to Laplace. I felt like I had no time to even think about it.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: I guess I mistook that for acceptance. After all, there's nothing I could do to change it.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Then about three months later, I broke my pen while writing a research log.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: I cried for 40 hours. FORTY HOURS. And I'm not exaggerating. I'm grateful my roommate didn't have me committed.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: Was it your parents' pen?
The very idea of Hissabeth crying seems almost impossible to imagine. She cuts off the thought before it turns impolite.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Nah. Just an ordinary Laplace office pen. They give them out by the box load.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: But back home when I broke something, my parents would tease me for being careless, and then we would find a new one together.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: You can't really accept a thing like this. The only thing you can do is put your pain aside and find something to do with yourself.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Even if it's just making a ball of tape. Just wrap a ball, round and round, over and over, until you've forgotten what it even looked like inside.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: Maybe that is something I can try.
The little astronaut nods solemnly.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Cool, you should. I'm speaking from my experience. You know, when you're young, everything bad seems like the end of the world. Forgetting your homework might as well be the apocalypse.
She's right. Name Day swallows the words he had meant to use to lighten the mood.
He's heard enough of them before. He's even asked himself the same.

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: Are you going home, Mr. Raccoon?

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: No, I'm heading out for a mission.

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: Vila said it's a time that you're familiar with, but that you didn't ever plan on going back.

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: I know Vila had another home before she moved to Rayashki. You must have one too!

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: What was it like? Does it snow there?

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: Yes. It snowed there, so much that it made the trees sag and covered up your footprints as soon as you walked past.

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: When the Volkhov froze over, my sister and I would go and fish from holes we cut in the ice.

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: Comrade Pasono once fell in the ice doing that. We didn't see him at school for weeks.

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: Playing on the ice can be dangerous, little Avgust.
Legend has it that girls who drown become Rusalki. He asked Vila once, and she confirmed it was only a myth.
Most stories are like that, heavily embellished in the retelling.
To hold the boy's drifting thoughts or rein in his own memories, he squats down until his head is level with the sunflower.

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: But it's all gone now. No matter the era, even if I went back to that little dot on the map, it would never be the same.

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: Like Rayashki.

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: Just like Rayashki.
Another patch of land whose story was lost to the "Storm." Remembered only by the few lucky enough to have lived there.
He tries to pull the topic back before it veers somewhere neither of them can handle.

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: That is why we must stay alive, then things will work out some day.
Lyonya, stay alive. That's the most important thing.
Keep going. Follow the route I told you. Never look back.

items.speaker: Foundation Registrar
items.text: Being certified as capable for an independent field mission means you're an official Foundation member. Congrats in advance.

items.speaker: Foundation Registrar
items.text: Most people here use an alias, though it's all up to you. Just make sure you pick a good one. It's not easy to change once it's confirmed.

items.speaker: Leonid
items.text: I see. Thank you for telling me.
The day he left home came close to another date soon to be celebrated.
That's it.
He hands over his application form.

items.speaker: Foundation Registrar
items.text: Let me check. Alright, no problem.

items.speaker: Foundation Registrar
items.text: The "Storm" has made everyone's life harder here. The Foundation is always in need of more manpower, and in need of honest men like you even more so.

items.speaker: Foundation Registrar
items.text: Welcome to the St. Pavlov Foundation Far East Branch, Mr. Name Day.
A name means existence.
What is hard to accept? Knowing that your city can't be found on any map, or that city still shares its name but has changed entirely.
He's tried before, but his arcane skill doesn't work on living beings. That fleeting glow he remembers is probably just an illusion.

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: You're thinking about something. Missing your home again, yes?

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: It's okay. Vila said as long as we pay attention in class and keep learning, we will be able to rebuild Rayashki in the future.

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: We will rebuild it as long as each and every comrade keeps that goal in their mind, and I will never forget.
The sunflower tilts its head. The boy mimics it, then he pats his friend's shoulder, offering a little encouragement.

items.speaker: Avgust
items.text: You can do it, Comrade Raccoon.

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: Thank you very, very much, Comrade Avgust.
Name Day is still lost in thought as the aurora begins to spill across the sky.
It follows its own patterns, constant and resplendent, existing without the need for names.
Nothing in nature is made for humanity.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Come here, Alia. You can have the best seat.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: Oh, I think for now, I'd prefer to be called Kiperina.
She mutters something more under her breath but still finds herself sitting in the offered spot.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Hurry up. You don't get an aurora like this every night.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: You need those charged particles up there for your arcane skill.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: I thought we were here for a vacation.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: It can be more than one thing. You do need this though.
She finds a suitable rock to sit on and brushes the dust off the stones beside her for Kiperina and Voyager.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Stay calm. Walking in space is definitely going to be easier than walking a tightrope.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: There's no absolute direction up there. Up or down depends on the reference you choose.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: In short, there's no "falling down."
Kiperina nods seriously.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: Tomorrow, no, the day after tomorrow, I'll be up there drifting above the Earth with the stars.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: I wonder if they'll feel warm to the touch.
Whether from nerves or the night wind, she shivers.
Hissabeth opens her arms wide to pull both girls into a huddle.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: The night is so cold. Back with the Utrennyaya, on nights like this, I would sneak into the pens and sleep beside Masha—the bear cub I took care of. She was so warm to cuddle.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: And now I'm here, huddled with all of you. Oh, sorry, I'm not suggesting you remind me of bears.

items.speaker: Kiperina
items.text: It just feels safe.

items.speaker: Name Day
items.text: There were times, during the coldest winter nights, that my siblings and I would cuddle up with the stray dogs to keep ourselves warm.

items.speaker: Han Zhang
items.text: Hold on. You people don't just hibernate through the winter? You're missing out.
This is the first time their little team has sat together without the mission on their minds, chatting instead about past lives and faraway memories.
Before she realizes it, sleepiness sneaks up on Kiperina.
She stands to shake off her sudden drowsiness, and Hissabeth rises with her.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Alright, we should head back. We don't want our little astronaut to be too tired.

items.speaker: Han Zhang
items.text: Hey, you think I don't see what you're doing? You haven't told us your story yet.

items.speaker: Han Zhang
items.text: It's been on my mind since I first got here: why would you do all this? You don't strike me as the hopeless dreamer type.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: I don't? Well, I should make more of an effort to match the stereotype.
She tilts her head just enough to catch the dozing little snake and nudge it back onto her shoulder.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: It's not so dreamy though. I just wanna know the answers. Where do we come from and how things will end?

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: What? Not convincing enough?

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Perhaps you want something more in-depth?

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Way back when, before all this, Pointer and I were being driven mad by work, we would walk out here and there was something she would say to me.
She narrows her eyes, watching the shifting curtains of light with interest.
High-energy solar particles, shaped by Earth's magnetic field, dance across the sky in colors visible to the naked eye.
If you listen closely, you might even hear their faint crackling.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Language is a tool that permits us to describe how the universe was created and how it will end.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Through it, we reflect on our existence. In order to understand eternity, we must first understand death and impermanence.
After a small shake of her head, she regains her usual casual tone.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: What do you think? Good impression of her, non? Everyone says it's my best.
The aurora hanging high above the sky shines down at the people below. Brilliant beams fall, blurring the edge between snow and sky and softening every expression into something unreadable.
Hissabeth's voice feels like it's coming from far away.

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: Tomorrow might be our last free day before the "Storm." I guess it's fitting then to ask the age-old question:

items.speaker: Hissabeth
items.text: If tomorrow was the last day of your life, what would you do?
